chapters.name: Chapter 1: Know where your money goes

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Making a simple monthly budget
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a monthly budget that shows your income, needs, wants and savings.
This lesson builds toward: Using last month's income and costs, you will write a monthly budget that sorts costs into needs, wants and savings, with a savings line and the total checked above or below zero.
A budget is a plan for your money. It answers two questions: how much money comes in each month, and where it goes. Without a plan, money tends to disappear on small things and the big bills feel like a surprise.
Start with income: pay after taxes, benefits such as Social Security or a pension, money from selling crops or goods, tips, or a sponsor payment. If your income changes from month to month, use the lowest normal month, so the plan still works in a slow month.
Then list your spending in three groups. Needs are what you must pay: housing, food, utilities, transport, medicine, minimum debt payments. Wants are nice but not required: eating out, new clothes, streaming services. Savings is money you set aside on purpose. Put savings in the plan like a bill, even if it is small.
If spending is bigger than income, cut wants first, then look for cheaper ways to meet needs. An AI assistant can help you make a blank budget table or suggest ways to cut costs, but type only rough amounts, never account numbers or passwords.
Step by step:
- Write your total monthly income after taxes. If it changes, use a low month.
- List your needs and what each costs a month.
- List your wants and what each costs a month.
- Choose a savings amount, even a small one.
- Subtract needs, wants and savings from income. If the answer is below zero, cut wants first.
- Check the plan at the end of the month and adjust.
Words to know:
- Budget: a plan for how you will use the money you get each month.
- Income: money that comes in: pay, benefits, sales, tips.
- Needs: costs you must pay to live and work, like rent, food and medicine.
- Wants: things that are nice to have but you could live without.
Official sources:
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Consumer tools and money guides
Try it now: On paper or in a free spreadsheet (Google Sheets or Excel), write last month's income and every cost you remember. Mark each cost N for need or W for want, add a savings line, and subtract. Is your answer above or below zero?
You can now write a monthly budget with income, needs, wants and savings, and see whether it adds up.

check.q: Which of these is a want, not a need?
check.why: A streaming service is nice to have; rent, medicine and transport to work are needs.

check.q: Your budget shows you spend more than you earn. What would you do first?
check.why: When a budget is below zero, wants are the first place to cut.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reading your credit report and score
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Get your free credit reports and check them for mistakes.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free credit report (AnnualCreditReport.com in the US), you will check every account on your credit report and dispute any mistakes, keeping copies of anything you send.
In the United States, a credit report is a record of how you have borrowed and paid: loans, credit cards, some bills, and accounts sent to collections. Lenders, landlords and some employers look at it. A credit score is a number made from that report that tries to predict whether you will pay on time.
You can get your credit reports free from the three nationwide companies, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, at AnnualCreditReport.com or by calling (877) 322-8228. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says you can now get them free once a week. Checking your own report does not hurt your score.
Be careful: some websites say "free credit report" but then sign you up for paid products. Use AnnualCreditReport.com.
Read each report and look for anything that is not yours: an account you never opened, a late payment you did make on time, a debt listed twice, or a wrong name or address. You have the right to dispute mistakes with the credit company and the business that reported them. Paying on time, keeping card balances low and not opening many new accounts at once all help your score over time.
Step by step:
- Go to AnnualCreditReport.com (type the address yourself) or call (877) 322-8228.
- Request your reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
- Check your name, addresses and every account.
- Circle anything you do not recognize or that is wrong.
- Dispute errors with the credit company, and keep copies of what you send.
Words to know:
- Credit report: a record of how you have borrowed money and paid it back.
- Credit score: a number made from your credit report that lenders use to judge risk.
- Dispute: to tell the credit company that something on your report is wrong and ask them to fix it.
- Collections: when a debt is sent to a company that tries to collect unpaid money.
Official sources:
- CFPB: How do I get a free copy of my credit reports?
- CFPB: Credit reports and scores
- AnnualCreditReport.com
Try it now: If you live in the US, request at least one free credit report at AnnualCreditReport.com and check every account on it. If you are outside the US, find out whether your country has a credit bureau and how to request your report from it. Write down one thing you checked and what you found.
You can now get your free credit reports, read them for mistakes, and know how to dispute an error.

options: A list of your bank passwords
A record of your loans, cards and payment history
check.why: A credit report lists your credit accounts and how you have paid them.

check.q: Your credit report shows an address where you never lived. What would you do?
options: Dispute it with the credit company and keep copies
Pay a stranger to fix it
check.why: Mistakes on a credit report should be disputed, with copies kept.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making a plan to pay down debt
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List your debts and choose which one to pay extra on first.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of debts, you will choose which debt to pay extra on using the highest-rate way or the smallest-balance way, while paying at least the minimum on every debt on time.
Debt is easier to beat when you can see all of it. Make a list of every debt: who you owe, how much, the interest rate, the minimum payment and the due date. Include credit cards, store cards, car loans, medical bills, loans from family, and any loan taken through a phone app.
Always pay at least the minimum on every debt, on time. Late payments add fees and can hurt your credit. Then put any extra money on just one debt at a time.
There are two common ways to choose. The highest-rate first way pays extra on the debt with the highest interest rate, which usually saves the most money. The smallest-balance first way pays off the smallest debt first, which gives a quick win and keeps many people going. Both work if you stick with them. When one debt is paid off, move its payment to the next one.
If you cannot make a payment, call the lender before the due date and ask about options. A nonprofit credit counselor can also help you make a plan. Be careful of companies that ask for big fees up front to "erase" your debt.
Step by step:
- List every debt: who, how much, interest rate, minimum, due date.
- Set up a way to pay every minimum on time, such as reminders.
- Choose one debt for extra payments: highest rate or smallest balance.
- When it is paid off, add its payment to the next debt.
- If you are going to miss a payment, call the lender before the due date.
Words to know:
- Interest rate: the price of borrowing, shown as a percent of what you owe.
- Minimum payment: the smallest amount you must pay each month to stay on time.
- Balance: how much you still owe.
Official sources:
- CFPB: Debt collection and managing debt
Try it now: Make a table of your debts (or a made-up example if you have none) with who, balance, rate, minimum and due date. Circle the debt you would pay extra on using the highest-rate way, and the one using the smallest-balance way.
You can now list your debts, pay the minimums on time, and choose which debt to pay extra on first.

check.q: What does the smallest-balance way of paying debt mean?
options: Pay only the smallest debt and skip the others
Pay extra on the debt with the smallest balance while paying minimums on the rest
Pay the same extra amount on every debt
Pay nothing until you have more money
check.why: You pay minimums on all and put extra on the smallest balance for a quick win.

check.q: You know you will miss a loan payment next week. What would you do?
options: Take a new loan to pay it
Call the lender before the due date and ask about options
check.why: Calling early gives you the most options.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Starting an emergency fund
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Set an emergency savings goal and an automatic way to reach it.
This lesson builds toward: Using your budget, you will set an emergency savings goal with an amount, a day and an automatic way to save, added as a line in your budget.
An emergency fund is money set aside only for surprises: a car repair, a doctor bill, a broken water pump, a lost shift or a slow sales month. Without it, a small problem can push you into expensive debt.
Start small. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says even a small amount gives some security. One way to pick a goal: think about surprise costs you had in the past year and what they cost. Then choose a first goal you can reach, and a bigger goal after that.
Make saving automatic. Set a regular transfer to savings on payday, or ask your employer to split your direct deposit if they allow it. Put tax refunds, cash gifts or part of a harvest payment straight into savings.
Keep the money somewhere safe but separate from spending money, such as a savings account at a bank or credit union. Cash at home can be lost or stolen. Decide in advance what counts as an emergency, use the fund when you need it, and then build it back up.
Step by step:
- Write down surprise costs you had in the last year.
- Choose a first goal you can reach and a bigger goal for later.
- Set an automatic transfer or a fixed amount you save every payday.
- Keep the fund separate from everyday spending money.
- Write what counts as an emergency. After you use it, rebuild it.
Words to know:
- Emergency fund: money kept only for unexpected costs or lost income.
- Automatic transfer: a payment your bank moves for you on a set day, without you doing it each time.
- Credit union: a not-for-profit bank owned by its members.
Official sources:
- CFPB: An essential guide to building an emergency fund
Try it now: Write your first emergency savings goal, the amount you will save each week or month, the day you will save it, and where you will keep it. Add it as a line in your Lesson 1 budget.
You can now set an emergency savings goal, save toward it automatically, and keep it safe and separate.

check.q: Which is an emergency an emergency fund is meant for?
options: A car repair you did not expect
check.why: Emergency funds cover unexpected costs, not planned wants.

check.q: You keep forgetting to save. What would you do?
options: Save only what is left at the end of the month
Set an automatic transfer on payday
check.why: Automatic saving on payday happens before the money is spent.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Saving with a bank, mobile money or a savings group
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a safe place to save and check its fees and rules before you use it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a bank, credit union, mobile money service or savings group, you will check the fees and rules before choosing a safe place to save, writing down what it costs to put money in and take it out.
Where you save matters. In the US, a savings account at a bank or credit union that is federally insured is one of the safest places for money. In many countries, especially in Africa, people save with mobile money on their phone, at a bank or SACCO, or in a savings group.
Mobile money services such as M-Pesa let you keep money on your phone, send it and pay bills. Many also have a separate savings or locked-savings option, which helps keep savings apart from spending money. Fees and interest are different for each service and change over time, so read the official fee table in the app or on the provider's website, or ask at an official agent, before you move money.
Example: a farmer in Kenya is paid for maize at harvest. She sends part of the payment into a separate savings option the same day, before she spends any, and leaves the rest for seeds, school fees and food. She checks the fee for each transfer in the official fee table first.
In a savings group, often called a chama, members each pay a set amount on a schedule. Write down every payment, keep a copy of the group's rules, and only join groups whose members you know and trust. Whatever you use: never share your PIN, and be careful of anyone who calls asking you to send money back after a "wrong" transfer. Check your balance first.
Step by step:
- Choose where to save: bank, credit union, SACCO, mobile money savings or a trusted savings group.
- Find the official fee table and rules, in the app, on the official website or from an official agent.
- Move savings on payday or harvest day, before spending.
- Keep a written record of every deposit.
- Never share your PIN, and check your balance before sending money back to anyone.
Words to know:
- Mobile money: a service that lets you store, send and receive money with a phone.
- SACCO: a savings and credit cooperative, a member-owned group that saves and lends, common in East Africa.
- Chama: a savings group, often in Kenya, where members save together on a schedule.
- PIN: a secret number that protects your account. Never share it.
Official sources:
- CFPB: An essential guide to building an emergency fund (where to keep savings)
Try it now: Pick the place you will keep your emergency savings. Find its official fee table or account rules and write down what it costs to put money in and take it out. If you use mobile money, find the savings option in the app menu without moving any money yet.
You can now choose a safe place to save, check its fees and rules first, and protect your account.

check.q: Why keep emergency savings in a bank or credit union instead of cash at home?
options: It is safer from theft and loss
Banks pay you to take money out
check.why: An account keeps savings safer than cash at home.

check.q: You plan to use a mobile money savings option. What would you do first?
options: Move all your money right away
Ask a stranger online what it costs
Read the official fee table and rules
check.why: Fees differ and change, so check the official fee table first.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Spotting predatory loans and money scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Read a loan or money offer and find the warning signs before you say yes.
This lesson builds toward: Given a loan or money offer, you will identify the warning signs of a predatory loan or scam before saying yes, finding every warning sign in the offer.
A predatory loan is a loan built to keep you paying. Payday loans, some car-title loans and some phone-app loans are short and very expensive. The fee may look small, but as an annual percentage rate (APR) the cost can be very high, and many people roll the loan over again and again. Before you borrow, look at the APR and every fee, and ask yourself how you will repay it.
Know your rights in the US: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says you cannot be arrested for not paying a payday loan, and a lender can take part of your pay only with a court order. Service members have extra protection under the Military Lending Act. You can also check whether a lender is licensed in your state.
Scams have warning signs. They rush you. They ask you to pay with gift cards, a wire transfer, cryptocurrency or a mobile money transfer to a stranger. They promise a loan or grant if you pay a fee first. They say you won a prize you never entered. They ask for your PIN, password or a code sent to your phone.
When you see a sign: stop, do not pay, and check with the real company using a number you find yourself. Talk to someone you trust. Cheaper options than a predatory loan can include asking the creditor for more time, a small loan from a credit union, or help from a local nonprofit.
Step by step:
- Find the APR and every fee in the offer.
- Ask: how and when will I repay this, and what if I cannot?
- Look for scam signs: rush, gift cards or wire, fee first, prize, PIN or code requests.
- Stop and check with the real company using a number you find yourself.
- Look for cheaper options: more time from the creditor, a credit union loan, a nonprofit.
Words to know:
- APR: annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of a loan, including fees, shown as a percent. It lets you compare loans.
- Payday loan: a small, short loan, often due on your next payday, that can be very expensive.
- Rollover: taking a new loan to pay off the old one, adding more fees.
- Predatory loan: a loan with unfair or very high costs that traps the borrower.
Official sources:
- CFPB: Payday loans
- CFPB: Fraud and scams
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page money plan: your Lesson 1 budget, your debt list with the debt you will pay extra on, your emergency savings goal and where you keep it, and the date you will check your credit reports. Then read one loan or money offer you have seen (a text, an ad or a letter) and write down every warning sign you find.
You can now read a loan or money offer, find the APR and the warning signs, and choose a safer option.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Monthly budget Income or costs are missing, or there is no savings line. Income, needs, wants and savings are listed and the total is checked. Uses a low, normal month and shows which wants were cut. Debt plan Debts are missing, or no debt is chosen for extra payments. All debts listed with balance, rate, minimum and due date, and one chosen for extra payments. Explains why they chose the highest-rate or smallest-balance way. Emergency savings No goal, or no amount and day. A goal, an amount, a day and a place to save, added to the budget. The saving is set up to happen automatically. Safe place to save Place chosen without checking fees or rules. Fees to put money in and take it out are written down from the official source. Compared two options before choosing. Credit report date No date to check credit reports. A date to check credit reports from the official free source. Has already checked one report and noted what they found. Offer warning signs Missed clear warning signs in the offer. Lists the warning signs in a real offer. Also names a safer option, such as a credit union loan. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a warning sign in a loan offer?
options: It asks you to pay a fee with a gift card to get the loan
It gives you time to read the terms
It comes from your credit union
check.why: Up-front fees paid with gift cards are a common scam sign.

check.q: A text says "You are pre-approved! Reply now or lose this offer today." What would you do?
options: Send your bank details to hold the offer
Slow down and check the lender through an official source before replying
check.why: Pressure to act now is a warning sign; check before you respond.
